opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a great question, and honestly one I think about a lot, because it's moving so fast. I think the biggest shift over the coming year won't necessarily come from some dramatic new architecture. It'll come from making these systems more reliable. Right now, a lot of agentic workflows work impressively in demos, but if you chain together ten or twenty steps, small error rates compound, and you end up with something that fails in ways that are hard to debug.

So I expect a lot of the progress to come from post-training. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards is a big part of that, especially for coding and tool use, where you can actually check whether the code ran, the tests passed, or the API call returned the right thing. We saw this with reasoning models, where training on verifiable tasks gave big jumps, and I think the same recipe gets applied more and more to multi-step, tool-using behavior.

The other area I'm watching is the tooling and scaffolding around the models. Things like better context management, memory, and deciding what to keep in the context window and what to summarize or offload. Long context is great, but performance still degrades when you stuff everything in there, so the systems that manage context well will have a real edge.

And practically, I think coding agents will stay the flagship use case, because the feedback loop is so tight. You write code, you run it, you see whether it works. That's a much friendlier environment for an agent than, say, open-ended web tasks, where it's hard to tell whether you succeeded.

One more thing I'd add: I'm hopeful we'll see more of this on the open-weight side too. Smaller models fine-tuned for specific agentic tasks can be surprisingly capable, and being able to run them locally matters a lot for privacy and cost. So I'd say the year ahead looks less like "agents suddenly do everything" and more like steady gains in reliability, plus agents getting really good in specific, well-defined domains. That's less flashy, but probably more useful.

r001.rationale: The response says progress will come less from new architectures and more from reliability, training, and tooling around models, framing advances largely as better agent systems built around LLMs.

r002.rationale: It mentions open-weight models, but does not contrast the open-weight community’s focus on developing models with OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s focus on tools around them.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a good question, and honestly it's one I think about a lot because I spend most of my time implementing these things from scratch, so I tend to look at it from the mechanics side rather than the hype side.

The short version is: I think the model capabilities are already mostly there for a lot of agentic use cases, and the bottleneck over the next year is going to be everything around the model. Tool interfaces, context management, evaluation, cost. If you look at what actually makes an agent fail today, it's rarely that the model can't reason about the step. It's that it loses track of state after thirty tool calls, or it confidently calls a tool with the wrong argument format, or nobody can tell whether the run was actually successful because the eval is "did a human look at it and nod."

So I'd expect a few things. One is consolidation around standard tool protocols, where the model just knows how to talk to a code interpreter, a file system, a browser, without every team re-inventing the glue. Second, I think we'll see a lot more emphasis on reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards specifically for multi-step tasks, coding being the obvious one because you can actually check the result. That's where the training side gets interesting, because now you're not just doing supervised fine-tuning on single turns, you're optimizing over trajectories, and that changes how you think about data.

And then the third thing, which is maybe less glamorous, is that smaller, more specialized models are going to do a lot of the actual work inside these systems. Not every step in a pipeline needs the frontier model. A lot of it is routing, parsing, checking, and a well-tuned small model is cheaper, faster, and often more predictable. I think a year from now the typical "agent" is actually a small orchestration of models rather than one giant one.

What I'm more skeptical about is the fully autonomous, go-run-my-business framing. I think the useful pattern for a while is going to be agents that do bounded tasks really well and hand back to a human at well-defined points. That's less exciting on a slide, but it's what actually ships.

r001.rationale: The response says model capabilities are already mostly sufficient and identifies improvements around the model—such as tools, context management, and evaluation—as the main bottleneck.

r002.rationale: The response does not contrast the open-weight community’s focus with OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s focus.

astra-6.text:
I think we’ll see a shift from models that just answer questions to systems that can carry out more of a task—write some code, run it, look at the result, and make a correction. Coding is a particularly useful setting for that because you have feedback. You can run tests and check whether a change worked.

The big question for me is reliability. A model can be very good at each individual step, but if you ask it to take twenty steps, those errors can accumulate. So I expect a lot of the progress to come from the surrounding system: how you give the model tools, how you check its work, and when you bring a human back into the loop.

Over the next year, I’m more excited about narrowly scoped agents that do a useful task consistently than a general-purpose agent that promises to do everything. If I can delegate something, review the result, and actually save time, that’s already a meaningful improvement.

r001.rationale: The response expects progress from tools, checking, and human oversight, but does not clearly frame advances as better use of existing LLMs rather than changes to the underlying models.

r002.rationale: It does not compare the open-weight or open-source community’s focus with OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s focus.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’ll see a shift from models that just generate answers toward systems that can actually carry out tasks over multiple steps. The interesting part is the loop: the model uses a tool, looks at the result, and decides what to do next.

Over the coming year, I expect the most useful progress to be in fairly well-defined workflows, like coding or working with documents, where you can check whether the result is correct. The challenge is reliability. If each step works most of the time, that doesn’t necessarily mean a long sequence of steps will work reliably.

So I’m especially interested in how we evaluate these systems, how they recover from mistakes, and when they ask for human input. Better models will help, but a lot of the improvement will also come from the systems around them—giving them the right tools, useful feedback, and a clear way to verify their work.

r001.rationale: The response describes improvements to the surrounding systems, but also says better models will help. It does not frame advances specifically as better use of existing LLMs rather than changes to the models.

r002.rationale: The response does not contrast the open-weight or open-source community’s focus with OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s focus.
